scenes.script_line: A raindrop lands on a worksite. Then it moves. Across the ground, into the soil or toward a ditch. It may eventually connect to a stream or lake. Water links places we think are separate. So when we protect water at a building site, we may be protecting much more than that site. Every drop has a journey.

shots.text: close-up of a single raindrop landing on bare worksite soil
wide shot of rainwater tracing a path toward a drainage ditch
medium shot of a worker checking a drainage channel near the site
close-up of water pooling near young plants at the site edge

scenes.script_line: You spend hours making a concrete finish perfect. Then, at the end, you wash the tools. Where does the dirty water go? Concrete washwater can be highly alkaline and harmful if released into the environment. A well-finished job needs a well-planned cleanup. Use the designated contained washout system. Quality continues after the last tool is put down.

shots.text: close-up of hands washing a trowel in a contained washout bucket
medium shot of a worker pouring washwater into a designated containment bin
wide shot of a finished concrete surface beside a sealed washout station
close-up of a labelled sign marking the concrete washout area

must_not: water poured directly onto bare soil

scenes.script_line: Turn on a tap. Water appears. It feels effortless. But behind that moment are collection, treatment, pipes and energy. On a dry Alentejo summer day, that resource deserves attention. The solution is not to stop using water. It is to use what we need and prevent unnecessary waste. Every careful action helps.

shots.text: close-up of a hand turning an outdoor tap
medium shot of a worker filling a watering can carefully, not overflowing
wide shot of a dry sunlit Alentejo-style field near the worksite
close-up of a water meter or hose fitting checked for leaks

scenes.script_line: Imagine a little oil leaking from a machine. It looks too small to matter. But rainwater can move pollutants beyond the original spot. What starts under one machine can become an environmental problem elsewhere. Report leaks early and let trained people contain them safely. A small problem noticed today can prevent a larger one tomorrow.

shots.text: close-up of a small oil stain beneath a parked machine
medium shot of a worker reporting a leak on a radio or to a supervisor
wide shot of a trained crew member containing a spill with absorbent mats
close-up of hands placing a drip tray under machinery

scenes.script_line: When we see a stream, we see moving water. But that water began elsewhere: rain, soil, slopes and tiny channels. Every part of the landscape contributes. That's why keeping rubbish, cement and chemicals out of drainage routes matters. The stream doesn't begin only where we can see it. Protecting water starts at the place where we work.

shots.text: wide shot of a small stream beginning among rocks and slopes
close-up of a drainage channel kept clear of rubbish near a worksite
medium shot of a worker clearing debris away from a drainage route
close-up of water flowing clean over stones in a small channel
